entries.3098c60491262c9a6071f8c9b0954525bae79ec1: <div sID="gen24785" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="11" osisID="Mark.11" sID="Mark.11"/> <div eID="gen24785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24786" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24787" type="x-p"/> We are now come to the Passion-Week, the week in which Christ died, and the great occurrences of that week. I. Christ's riding in triumph into Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Mark.11.1-Mark.11.11">ver. 1-11</reference>. II. His cursing the barren fig-tree, <reference osisRef="Mark.11.12-Mark.11.14">ver. 12-14</reference>. III. His driving those out of the temple that turned it into an exchange, <reference osisRef="Mark.11.15-Mark.11.19">ver. 15-19</reference>. IV. His discourse with his disciples concerning the power of faith and the efficacy of prayer, on occasion of the withering of the fig-tree he cursed, <reference osisRef="Mark.11.20-Mark.11.26">ver. 20-26</reference>. V. His reply to those who questioned his authority, <reference osisRef="Mark.11.27-Mark.11.33">ver. 27-33</reference>.
entries.e75eea2fc1c1d6cf0aed1ce75ecb17548fa041ca: <div eID="gen24787" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24786" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Entrance into Jerusalem.</title> <div sID="gen24788" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And when they came nigh to Jerusalem, unto Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount of Olives, he sendeth forth two of his disciples, <hi type="super">2</hi> And saith unto them, Go your way into the village over against you: and as soon as ye be entered into it, ye shall find a colt tied, whereon never man sat; loose him, and bring <hi type="italic">him.</hi> <hi type="super">3</hi> And if any man say unto you, Why do ye this? say ye that the Lord hath need of him; and straightway he will send him hither. <hi type="super">4</hi> And they went their way, and found the colt tied by the door without in a place where two ways met; and they loose him. <hi type="super">5</hi> And certain of them that stood there said unto them, What do ye, loosing the colt? <hi type="super">6</hi> And they said unto them even as Jesus had commanded: and they let them go. 7 And they brought the colt to Jesus, and cast their garments on him; and he sat upon him. <hi type="super">8</hi> And many spread their garments in the way: and others cut down branches off the trees, and strawed <hi type="italic">them</hi> in the way. <hi type="super">9</hi> And they that went before, and they that followed, cried, saying, Hosanna; Blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> he that cometh in the name of the Lord: <hi type="super">10</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the kingdom of our father David, that cometh in the name of the Lord: Hosanna in the highest. <hi type="super">11</hi> And Jesus entered into Jerusalem, and into the temple: and when he had looked round about upon all things, and now the eventide was come, he went out unto Bethany with the twelve. <div eID="gen24788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24789" type="x-p"/> We have here the story of the public entry Christ made into Jerusalem, four or five days before his death. And he came into town thus remarkably, 1. To show that he was not afraid of the power and malice of his enemies in Jerusalem. He did not steal into the city <hi type="italic">incognito,</hi> as one that durst not show his face; no, they needed not send spies to search for him, he comes in with observation. This would be an encouragement to his disciples that were timorous, and cowed at the thought of their enemies' power and rage; let them see how bravely their Master sets them all at defiance. 2. To show that he was not cast down or disquieted at the thoughts of his approaching sufferings. He came, not only publicly, but cheerfully, and with acclamations of joy. Though he was now but taking the field, and <hi type="italic">girding on the harness,</hi> yet, being fully assured of a complete victory, he thus triumphs as though he had put it off. <div eID="gen24789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24790" type="x-p"/> I. The <hi type="italic">outside</hi> of this triumph was very <hi type="italic">mean;</hi> he rode upon an ass's <hi type="italic">colt,</hi> which being an ass, looked contemptible, and made no figure; and, being but a <hi type="italic">colt, whereon never man sat,</hi> we may suppose, was rough and untrimmed, and not only so, but rude and ungovernable, and would disturb and disgrace the solemnity. This <hi type="italic">colt</hi> was borrowed too. Christ went upon the water in a <hi type="italic">borrowed</hi> boat, ate the passover in a <hi type="italic">borrowed</hi> chamber, was buried in a <hi type="italic">borrowed</hi> sepulchre, and here rode on a <hi type="italic">borrowed</hi> ass. Let not Christians scorn to be beholden one to another, and, when need is, to go a borrowing, for our Master did not. He had no rich trappings; they threw their clothes upon the colt, and so he <hi type="italic">sat upon him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.11.7">v. 7</reference>. The persons that attended, were mean people; and all the show they could make, was, by <hi type="italic">spreading their garments in the way</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.8">v. 8</reference>), as they used to do at the feast of tabernacles. All these were marks of his humiliation; even when he would be taken notice of, he would be taken notice of for his meanness; and they are instructions to us, not to <hi type="italic">mind high things,</hi> but to <hi type="italic">condescend to them of low estate.</hi> How ill doth it become Christians to <hi type="italic">take state,</hi> when Christ was so far from affecting it! <div eID="gen24790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24791" type="x-p"/> II. The <hi type="italic">inside</hi> of this triumph was very <hi type="italic">great;</hi> not only as it was the fulfilling of the scripture (which is not taken notice of here, as it as in Matthew), but as there were several rays of Christ's glory shining forth in the midst of all this meanness. 1. Christ showed his knowledge of things distant, and his power over the wills of men, when he sent his disciples for the colt, <reference osisRef="Mark.11.1-Mark.11.3">v. 1-3</reference>. By this it appears that he can <hi type="italic">do every thing,</hi> and <hi type="italic">no thought can be withholden from him.</hi> 2. He showed his dominion over the <hi type="italic">creatures</hi> in riding on <hi type="italic">a colt that was never backed.</hi> The subjection of the inferior part of the creation to man is spoken of with application to Christ (<reference osisRef="Ps.8.5-Ps.8.6">Ps. viii. 5, 6</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="Heb.2.8">Heb. ii. 8</reference>); for to him it is owing, and to his mediation, that we have any remaining benefit by the grant God made to man, of a sovereignty in this lower world, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.28">Gen. i. 28</reference>. And perhaps Christ, in riding the ass's colt, would give a shadow of his power over the spirit of man, who is born as the <hi type="italic">wild ass's colt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.11.12">Job xi. 12</reference>. 3. The colt was brought from a place <hi type="italic">where two ways met</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.4">v. 4</reference>), as if Christ would show that he came to direct those into the right way, who had <hi type="italic">two ways</hi> before them, and were in danger of taking the wrong. 4. Christ received the joyful <hi type="italic">hosannas</hi> of the people; that is, both the <hi type="italic">welcome</hi> they gave him and their <hi type="italic">good wishes</hi> to the prosperity of his kingdom, <reference osisRef="Mark.11.9">v. 9</reference>. It was God that put it into the hearts of these people to cry <hi type="italic">Hosanna,</hi> who were not by art and management brought to it, as those were who afterward cried, <hi type="italic">Crucify, crucify.</hi> Christ reckons himself honoured by the faith and praises of the multitude, and it is God that brings people to do him this honour beyond their own intentions. <div eID="gen24791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24792" type="x-p"/> (1.) They <hi type="italic">welcomed</hi> his <hi type="italic">person</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.9">v. 9</reference>); <hi type="italic">Blessed is he that cometh,</hi> the <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ho erchomenos</hi></hi>, <hi type="italic">he that should come,</hi> so often promised, so long expected; he comes <hi type="italic">in the name of the Lord,</hi> as God's Ambassador to the world; <hi type="italic">Blessed be he:</hi> let him have our applauses, and best affections; he is a <hi type="italic">blessed</hi> Saviour, and brings blessings to us, and blessed be he that sent him. Let him be <hi type="italic">blessed in the name of the Lord,</hi> and let all nations and ages call him <hi type="italic">Blessed,</hi> and think and speak highly and honourably of him. <div eID="gen24792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24793" type="x-p"/> (2.) They <hi type="italic">wished well</hi> to his <hi type="italic">intent,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.11.10">v. 10</reference>. They believed that, mean a figure as he made, he had a <hi type="italic">kingdom,</hi> which should shortly be set up in the world, that it was the kingdom of <hi type="italic">their father David</hi> (that father of his country), the kingdom promised to him and his seed for ever; a kingdom that came <hi type="italic">in the name of the Lord,</hi> supported by a divine authority. <hi type="italic">Blessed be this kingdom;</hi> let it take place, let it get ground, let it come in the power of it, and let all opposing rule, principality, and power, be put down; let it go on <hi type="italic">conquering, and to conquer.</hi> <hi type="italic">Hosanna</hi> to this kingdom; prosperity be to it; all happiness attend it. The proper signification of <hi type="italic">hosanna</hi> is that which we find, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.10">Rev. vii. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">Salvation to our God, that sitteth on the throne, and to the Lamb;</hi> success to religion, both <hi type="italic">natural</hi> and <hi type="italic">revealed, Hosanna in the highest.</hi> Praises be to our God, who is in the <hi type="italic">highest heavens</hi> over all, God blessed for ever; or, Let him be praised by his angels, that are <hi type="italic">in the highest</hi> heavens, let our <hi type="italic">hosannas</hi> be an echo to theirs. <div eID="gen24793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24794" type="x-p"/> Christ, thus <hi type="italic">attended,</hi> thus <hi type="italic">applauded,</hi> came into the city, and went directly <hi type="italic">to the temple.</hi> Here was no banquet of wine prepared for his entertainment, nor the least refreshment; but he immediately applied himself to his work, for that was his <hi type="italic">meat</hi> and <hi type="italic">drink.</hi> He went <hi type="italic">to the temple,</hi> that the scripture might be fulfilled; "<hi type="italic">The Lord whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple,</hi> without sending any immediate notice before him; he shall surprise you with a <hi type="italic">day of visitation,</hi> for he shall be <hi type="italic">like a refiner's fire, and like fuller's soap,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Mal.3.1-Mal.3.3">Mal. iii. 1-3</reference>. He came to the temple, and took a view of the present state of it, <reference osisRef="Mark.11.11">v. 11</reference>. He <hi type="italic">looked round about upon all things,</hi> but as yet said nothing. He saw many disorders there, but <hi type="italic">kept silence,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.21">Ps. l. 21</reference>. Though he intended to suppress them, he would not go about the doing of it all <hi type="italic">on a sudden,</hi> lest he should seem to have done it <hi type="italic">rashly;</hi> he let things be as they were for this night, intending the next morning to apply himself to the necessary reformation, and to take the day before him. We may be confident that God sees all the wickedness that is in the world, though he do not presently reckon for it, nor cast it out. Christ, having make his remarks upon what he saw in the temple, retired in the evening to a friend's house at Bethany, because there he would be more out of the noise of the town, and out of the way of being suspected, a designing to head a faction.
entries.2c5158dc30d4374e4ec5a23460432ad31cf328ab: <div eID="gen24794" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Barren Fig-Tree Cursed.</title> <div sID="gen24795" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> And on the morrow, when they were come from Bethany, he was hungry: <hi type="super">13</hi> And seeing a fig tree afar off having leaves, he came, if haply he might find any thing thereon: and when he came to it, he found nothing but leaves; for the time of figs was not <hi type="italic">yet.</hi> <hi type="super">14</hi> And Jesus answered and said unto it, No man eat fruit of thee hereafter for ever. And his disciples heard <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">15</hi> And they come to Jerusalem: and Jesus went into the temple, and began to cast out them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves; <hi type="super">16</hi> And would not suffer that any man should carry <hi type="italic">any</hi> vessel through the temple. <hi type="super">17</hi> And he taught, saying unto them, Is it not written, My house shall be called of all nations the house of prayer? but ye have made it a den of thieves. <hi type="super">18</hi> And the scribes and chief priests heard <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and sought how they might destroy him: for they feared him, because all the people was astonished at his doctrine. <hi type="super">19</hi> And when even was come, he went out of the city. <hi type="super">20</hi> And in the morning, as they passed by, they saw the fig tree dried up from the roots. <hi type="super">21</hi> And Peter calling to remembrance saith unto him, Master, behold, the fig tree which thou cursedst is withered away. <hi type="super">22</hi> And Jesus answering saith unto them, Have faith in God. <hi type="super">23</hi> For verily I say unto you, That whosoever shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea; and shall not doubt in his heart, but shall believe that those things which he saith shall come to pass; he shall have whatsoever he saith. <hi type="super">24</hi> Therefore I say unto you, What things soever ye desire, when ye pray, believe that ye receive <hi type="italic">them,</hi> and ye shall have <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">25</hi> And when ye stand praying, forgive, if ye have ought against any: that your Father also which is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses. <hi type="super">26</hi> But if ye do not forgive, neither will your Father which is in heaven forgive your trespasses. <div eID="gen24795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24796" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Christ's cursing the fruitless fig-tree. He had a convenient resting-place at Bethany, and therefore thither he went at resting-time; but his work lay at Jerusalem, and thither therefore he returned in the morning, at working-time; and so intent was he upon his work, that he went out from Bethany without breakfast, which, before he was gone far, he found the want of, and <hi type="italic">was hungry</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.12">v. 12</reference>), for he was subject to all the sinless infirmities of our nature. Finding himself in want of food, he went to a <hi type="italic">fig-tree,</hi> which he saw at some distance, and which being well <hi type="italic">adorned</hi> with green leaves he hoped to find <hi type="italic">enriched</hi> with some sort of fruit. But he <hi type="italic">found nothing but leaves;</hi> he hoped to find some fruit, <hi type="italic">for</hi> though <hi type="italic">the time of</hi> gathering in <hi type="italic">figs</hi> was near, it <hi type="italic">was not yet;</hi> so that it could not be pretended that it had had fruit, but that it was gathered and gone; for the season had not yet arrived. Or, He found none, for indeed <hi type="italic">it was not a season of figs,</hi> it was no good fig-year. But this was worse than any fig-tree, for there was not so much as one fig to be found upon it, though it was so full of leaves. However, Christ was willing to make an example of it, not to the <hi type="italic">trees,</hi> but to the <hi type="italic">men,</hi> of that generation, and therefore cursed it with that curse which is the reverse of the first blessing, <hi type="italic">Be fruitful;</hi> he said unto it, <hi type="italic">Never let any man eat fruit of thee hereafter for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.11.14">v. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">Sweetness and good fruit</hi> are, in Jotham's parable, the honour of the <hi type="italic">fig-tree</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.9.11">Judg. ix. 11</reference>), and its serviceableness therein to man, preferable to the preferment of being <hi type="italic">promoted over the trees;</hi> now to be deprived of that, was a grievous <hi type="italic">curse.</hi> This was intended to be a type and figure of the doom passed upon the Jewish church, to which he came, <hi type="italic">seeking fruit, but found none</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.13.6-Luke.13.7">Luke xiii. 6, 7</reference>); and though it was not, according to the doom in the parable, immediately cut down, yet, according to this in the history, <hi type="italic">blindness</hi> and <hi type="italic">hardness</hi> befel them (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.8">Rom. xi. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.25">25</reference>), so that they were from henceforth <hi type="italic">good for nothing.</hi> The <hi type="italic">disciples heard</hi> what sentence Christ passed on this tree, and took notice of it. Woes from Christ's mouth are to be observed and kept in mind, as well as blessings. <div eID="gen24796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24797" type="x-p"/> II. His clearing the temple of the market-people that frequented it, and of those that made it a thoroughfare. We do not find that Christ met with food elsewhere, when he missed of it on the fig-tree; but the zeal of God's house so ate him up, and made him forget himself, that he came, hungry as he was, to Jerusalem, and went straight to the temple, and began to reform those abuses which the day before he had marked out; to show that when the Redeemer came to Zion, his errand was, <hi type="italic">to turn away ungodliness from Jacob</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Rom. xi. 26</reference>), and that he came not, as he was falsely accused, to <hi type="italic">destroy</hi> the temple, but to purify and refine it, and reduce his church to its primitive rectitude. <div eID="gen24797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24798" type="x-p"/> 1. He cast out the <hi type="italic">buyers</hi> and <hi type="italic">sellers, overthrew the tables of the money-changers</hi> (and threw the money to the ground, the fitter place for it), and threw down the <hi type="italic">seats of them that sold doves.</hi> This he did as one having authority, as <hi type="italic">a Son in his own house.</hi> The filth of the daughter of Zion is purged away, not by might, nor by power, but by <hi type="italic">the spirit of judgment, and the spirit of burning.</hi> And he did it without opposition; for what he did, was manifested to be right and good, even in the consciences of those that had connived at it, and countenanced it, because they got money by it. Note, It may be some encouragement to zealous reformers, that frequently the purging out of corruptions, and the correcting of abuses, prove an easier piece of work than was apprehended. Prudent attempts sometimes prove successful beyond expectation, and there are not those lions <hi type="italic">found</hi> in the way, that were feared to be. <div eID="gen24798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24799" type="x-p"/> 2. He <hi type="italic">would not suffer that any man should carry any vessel,</hi> any sort of goods or wares, <hi type="italic">through the temple,</hi> or any of the courts of it, because it was the nearer way, and would save them the labour of going about, <reference osisRef="Mark.11.16">v. 16</reference>. The Jews owned that it was one of the instances of honour due to the temple, not to make the mountain of the house, or the court of the Gentiles, a road, or common passage, or to come into it with any bundle. <div eID="gen24799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24800" type="x-p"/> 3. He gave a good reason for this; because it was written, <hi type="italic">My house shall be called of all nations, The house of prayer,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.11.17">v. 17</reference>. So it is written, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.7">Isa. lvi. 7</reference>. It shall pass among all people under that character. <hi type="italic">It shall be the house of prayer to all nations;</hi> it was so in the first institution of it; when Solomon dedicated it, it was with an eye to the sons of the strangers, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.41">1 Kings viii. 41</reference>. And it was prophesied that it should be yet more so. Christ will have the temple, as a type of the gospel-church, to be, (1.) A <hi type="italic">house of prayer.</hi> After he had turned out the oxen and doves, which were things for sacrifice, he revived the appointment of it as a <hi type="italic">house of prayer,</hi> to teach us that when all sacrifices and offerings should be abolished, the spiritual sacrifices of prayer and praise should continue and remain for ever. (2.) That it should be so <hi type="italic">to all nations,</hi> and not to the people of the Jews only; for <hi type="italic">whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord, shall be saved,</hi> though not of the seed of Jacob, according to the flesh. It was therefore insufferable for them to <hi type="italic">make it a den of thieves,</hi> which would prejudice those nations against it, whom they should have invited to it. When Christ drove out the buyers and sellers at the beginning of his ministry, he only charged them with making the temple a <hi type="italic">house of merchandise</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.2.16">John ii. 16</reference>); but now he chargeth them with making it a <hi type="italic">den of thieves,</hi> because since then they had twice gone about to stone him in the temple (<reference osisRef="John.8.59">John viii. 59</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.31">x. 31</reference>), or because the traders there were grown notorious for cheating their customers, and imposing upon the ignorance and necessity of the country people, which is no better than downright thievery. Those that suffer vain worldly thoughts to lodge within them when they are at their devotions, turn the <hi type="italic">house of prayer</hi> into a <hi type="italic">house of merchandise;</hi> but they that make long prayers for pretence to devour widows' houses, turn it into a <hi type="italic">den of thieves.</hi> <div eID="gen24800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24801" type="x-p"/> 4. The scribes and the chief priests were extremely nettled at this, <reference osisRef="Mark.11.18">v. 18</reference>. They hated him, and hated to be reformed by him; and yet they <hi type="italic">feared him,</hi> lest he should next overthrow <hi type="italic">their</hi> seats, and expel <hi type="italic">them,</hi> being conscious to themselves of the profaning and abusing of their power. They found that he had a great interest, that <hi type="italic">all the people were astonished at his doctrine,</hi> and that every thing he said, was an oracle and a law to them; and what durst <hi type="italic">he</hi> not attempt, what could <hi type="italic">he</hi> not effect, being thus supported? They therefore sought, not how he might make their peace with him, but <hi type="italic">how they might destroy him.</hi> A desperate attempt, and which, one would think, they themselves could not but fear was <hi type="italic">fighting against God.</hi> But they care not what they do, to support their own power and grandeur. <div eID="gen24801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24802" type="x-p"/> III. His discourse with his disciples, upon occasion of the fig-tree's withering away which he had cursed. At <hi type="italic">even,</hi> as usual, he <hi type="italic">went out of the city</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.19">v. 19</reference>), to Bethany; but it is probable that it was in the dark, so that they could not see the fig-tree; but the next morning, as they <hi type="italic">passed by,</hi> they observed the <hi type="italic">fig-tree dried up from the roots,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.11.20">v. 20</reference>. More is <hi type="italic">included</hi> many times in Christ's curses than is <hi type="italic">expressed,</hi> as appears by the effects of them. The curse was no more than that it should never bear fruit again, but the effect goes further, <hi type="italic">it is dried up from the roots.</hi> If it bear no fruit, it shall bear no leaves to cheat people. Now observe, <div eID="gen24802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24803" type="x-p"/> 1. How the disciples were affected with it. Peter remembered Christ's words, and said, with surprise, <hi type="italic">Master, behold, the fig-tree which thou cursedst is withered away,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.11.21">v. 21</reference>. Note, Christ's curses have wonderful effects, and make those to wither presently, that flourished like the green bay-tree. <hi type="italic">Those whom he curseth are cursed indeed.</hi> This represented the character and state of the Jewish church; which, from henceforward, was a tree dried up from the roots; no longer fit for food, but for fuel only. The first establishment of the Levitical priesthood was ratified and confirmed by the miracle of a <hi type="italic">dry rod,</hi> which in <hi type="italic">one night</hi> budded, and blossomed, and brought forth almonds (<reference osisRef="Num.17.8">Num. xvii. 8</reference>), a happy omen of the fruitlessness and flourishing of that priesthood. And now, by a contrary miracle, the expiration of that priesthood was signified by a flourishing tree dried up in a night; the just punishment of those priests that had abused it. And this seemed very strange to the disciples, and scarcely credible, that the Jews, who had been so long God's own, his only professing people in the world, should be thus abandoned; they could not imagine how that <hi type="italic">fig-tree</hi> should <hi type="italic">so soon wither away:</hi> but this comes of rejecting Christ, and being rejected by him. <div eID="gen24803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24804" type="x-p"/> 2. The good instructions Christ gave them from it; for of <hi type="italic">those</hi> even this <hi type="italic">withered</hi> tree was <hi type="italic">fruitful.</hi> <div eID="gen24804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24805" type="x-p"/> (1.) Christ teacheth them from hence to <hi type="italic">pray in faith</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.22">v. 22</reference>); <hi type="italic">Have faith in God.</hi> They admired the power of Christ's word of command; "Why," said Christ, "a lively active faith would put as great a power into your prayers, <reference osisRef="Mark.11.23-Mark.11.24">v. 23, 24</reference>. <hi type="italic">Whosoever shall say to this mountain,</hi> this mount of Olives, <hi type="italic">Be removed, and be cast into the sea;</hi> if he has but any word of God, general or particular, to build his faith upon, and if he <hi type="italic">shall not doubt in his heart, but shall believe that those things which he saith,</hi> according to the warrant he has from what God hath said, <hi type="italic">shall come to pass, he shall have whatsoever he saith.</hi>" Through the strength and power of God in Christ, the greatest difficulty shall be got over, and the thing shall be effected. And therefore (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.24">v. 24</reference>), "<hi type="italic">What things soever ye desire, when ye pray believe that ye shall</hi> receive them; nay, believe that ye <hi type="italic">do receive them,</hi> and he that has power to give them, saith, <hi type="italic">Ye shall have them. I say unto you,</hi> Ye shall, <reference osisRef="Mark.11.24">v. 24</reference>. <hi type="italic">Verily</hi> I say unto you, Ye shall," <reference osisRef="Mark.11.23">v. 23</reference>. Now this is to be applied, [1.] To that <hi type="italic">faith of miracles</hi> which the apostles and first preachers of the gospel were endued with, which did wonders in <hi type="italic">things natural,</hi> healing the sick, raising the dead, casting out devils; these were, in effect, the removing of mountains. The apostles speak of a faith which would do that, and yet might be found where holy love was not, <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.2">1 Cor. xiii. 2</reference>. [2.] It may be applied to that <hi type="italic">miracle of faith,</hi> which all true Christians are endued with, which doeth wonders in <hi type="italic">things spiritual.</hi> <hi type="italic">It justifies</hi> us (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.1">Rom. v. 1</reference>), and so removes the mountains of guilt, and casts them into the <hi type="italic">depths of the sea,</hi> never to rise up in judgment against us, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.19">Mic. vii. 19</reference>. It <hi type="italic">purifies</hi> the heart (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.9">Acts xv. 9</reference>), and so removes mountains of corruption, and <hi type="italic">makes them plains</hi> before the grace of God, <reference osisRef="Zech.4.7">Zech. iv. 7</reference>. It is by faith that the world is conquered, Satan's fiery darts are quenched, a soul is crucified with Christ, and yet lives; by faith we set the Lord always before us, and see him that is invisible, and have him present to our minds; and this is effectual to remove mountains, for at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob, the mountains were not only moved, but <hi type="italic">re</hi>moved, <reference osisRef="Ps.114.4-Ps.114.7">Ps. cxiv. 4-7</reference>. <div eID="gen24805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24806" type="x-p"/> (2.) To this is added here that necessary qualification of the prevailing prayer, that we freely forgive those who have been any way injurious to us, and be in charity with all men (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.25-Mark.11.26">v. 25, 26</reference>); <hi type="italic">When ye stand praying,</hi> forgive. Note, Standing is no improper posture for prayer; it was generally used among the Jews; hence they called their prayers, their <hi type="italic">standings;</hi> when they would say how the world was <hi type="italic">kept up</hi> by prayer, they expressed it thus, <hi type="italic">Stationibus stat mundus—The world is held up by standings.</hi> But the primitive Christians generally used more humble and reverent gesture of kneeling, especially on fast days, though not on Lord's days. When we are at prayer, we must remember to pray for others, particularly for our enemies, and those that have wronged us; now we cannot pray sincerely that God would do them good, if we bear malice to them, and wish them ill. If we have injured others before we pray, we must go and <hi type="italic">be reconciled to them;</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.23-Matt.5.24">Matt. v. 23, 24</reference>. But if they have injured us, we go a nearer way to work, and must immediately from our hearts <hi type="italic">forgive</hi> them. [1.] Because this is a <hi type="italic">good step</hi> towards obtaining the <hi type="italic">pardon</hi> of our own sins: <hi type="italic">Forgive,</hi> that <hi type="italic">your Father may forgive you;</hi> that is, "that he may be qualified to receive forgiveness, that he may forgive you without injury to his honour, as it would be, if he should suffer those to have such benefit by his mercy, as are so far from being conformable to the pattern of it." [2.] Because the want of this is a certain bar to the obtaining of the pardon of our sins; "<hi type="italic">If ye do not forgive</hi> those who have injured you, if he hate their persons, bear them a grudge, meditate revenge, and take all occasion to speak ill of them, <hi type="italic">neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.</hi>" This ought to be remembered in prayer, because one great errand we have to the throne of grace, is, to pray for the pardon of our sins: and care about it ought to be our daily care, because prayer is a part of our daily work. Our Saviour often insists on this, for it was his great design to engage his disciples to love one another.
entries.82fd585027b0c45081cbc39abfdbbc3668a4e80d: <div eID="gen24806" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Pharisees Nonplussed.</title> <div sID="gen24807" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> And they come again to Jerusalem: and as he was walking in the temple, there come to him the chief priests, and the scribes, and the elders, <hi type="super">28</hi> And say unto him, By what authority doest thou these things? and who gave thee this authority to do these things? <hi type="super">29</hi> And Jesus answered and said unto them, I will also ask of you one question, and answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things. <hi type="super">30</hi> The baptism of John, was <hi type="italic">it</hi> from heaven, or of men? answer me. 31 And they reasoned with themselves, saying, If we shall say, From heaven; he will say, Why then did ye not believe him? 32 But if we shall say, Of men; they feared the people: for all <hi type="italic">men</hi> counted John, that he was a prophet indeed. <hi type="super">33</hi> And they answered and said unto Jesus, We cannot tell. And Jesus answering saith unto them, Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things. <div eID="gen24807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24808" type="x-p"/> We have here Christ examined by the great Sanhedrim concerning his authority; for they claimed a power to call prophets to an account concerning their mission. They came to him when he was <hi type="italic">walking in the temple,</hi> not for his diversion, but <hi type="italic">teaching</hi> the people, first one company and then another. The Peripatetic philosophers were so called from the custom they had of <hi type="italic">walking</hi> when they taught. The cloisters, or piazzas, in the courts of the temple, were fitted for this purpose. The great men were vexed to see him followed and heard with attention, and therefore <hi type="italic">came to him</hi> with some solemnity, and did as it were arraign him at the bar with this question, <hi type="italic">By what authority doest thou these things?</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.11.28">v. 28</reference>. Now observe, <div eID="gen24808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24809" type="x-p"/> I. How they designed hereby to run him aground, and embarrass him. If they could make it out before the people, that he had not a <hi type="italic">legal mission,</hi> that he was not duly <hi type="italic">ordained,</hi> though he was ever so well qualified, and preached ever so profitably and well, they would tell the people that they <hi type="italic">ought not to hear him.</hi> This they made the last refuge of an obstinate unbelief; because they were resolved not to receive his doctrine, they were resolved to find some flaw or other in his commission, and will conclude it invalid, if it be not produced and ratified in their court. Thus the Papists resolve their controversy with us very much into the mission of our ministers, and if they have but any pretence to overthrow that, they think they have gained their point, though we have the scripture ever so much on our side. But this is indeed a question, which all that act either as magistrates or ministers, ought to be furnished with a good answer to, and often put to themselves, <hi type="italic">By what authority do I these things?</hi> For <hi type="italic">how can men preach except they be sent?</hi> Or how can they act with comfort, or confidence, or hope of success, except they be authorized? <reference osisRef="Jer.23.32">Jer. xxiii. 32</reference>. <div eID="gen24809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24810" type="x-p"/> II. How he effectually ran them aground, and embarrassed them, with this question, "What are your thoughts concerning <hi type="italic">the baptism of John?</hi> <hi type="italic">Was it from heaven, or of men?</hi> By what authority did John preach, and baptize, and gather disciples? <hi type="italic">Answer me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.11.30">v. 30</reference>. Deal fairly and ingenuously, and give a categorical answer, one way or the other." By this resolve of <hi type="italic">their</hi> question into <hi type="italic">this,</hi> our Saviour intimates how near akin his doctrine and baptism were to John's; they had the same original, and the same design and tendency—to introduce the gospel kingdom. Christ might with the better grace put this question to <hi type="italic">them,</hi> because they had sent a committee of their own house to examine John, <reference osisRef="John.1.19">John i. 19</reference>. "Now," saith Christ, "what was the result of your enquiries concerning him?" <div eID="gen24810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24811" type="x-p"/> They knew what they <hi type="italic">thought</hi> of this question; they could not but think that <hi type="italic">John Baptist</hi> was a man sent of God. But the difficulty was, what they should <hi type="italic">say to it</hi> now. Men that oblige not themselves to speak <hi type="italic">as they think</hi> (which is a certain rule) cannot avoid perplexing themselves thus. <div eID="gen24811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24812" type="x-p"/> 1. If they own the baptism of John to be <hi type="italic">from heaven,</hi> as really it was, they <hi type="italic">shame themselves;</hi> for Christ will presently turn it upon them, <hi type="italic">Why did ye not then believe him,</hi> and receive his baptism? They could not bear that Christ should say this, but they could bear it that their own consciences should say so, because they had an art of stifling and silencing them, and because what conscience said, though it might gall and grate them a little, would not <hi type="italic">shame them;</hi> and then <hi type="italic">they</hi> would do well enough, who looked no further than Saul's care, when he was convicted, <hi type="italic">Honour me now before this people,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.30">1 Sam. xv. 30</reference>. <div eID="gen24812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24813" type="x-p"/> 2. If they say, "<hi type="italic">It is of men,</hi> he was not sent of God, but his doctrine and baptism were inventions of his own," they <hi type="italic">expose themselves,</hi> the people will be ready to do them a mischief, or a least clamour upon them; for <hi type="italic">all men counted John that he was a prophet indeed,</hi> and therefore they could not bear that he should be reflected on. Note, There is a carnal slavish fear, which not only wicked subjects but wicked rulers likewise are liable to, which God makes use of as a means to keep the world in some order, and to suppress <hi type="italic">violence,</hi> that it shall not always <hi type="italic">grow up into a rod of wickedness.</hi> Now by this dilemma to which Christ brought them, (1.) They were confounded and baffled, and forced to make a dishonourable retreat; to pretend ignorance—<hi type="italic">We cannot tell</hi> (and that was mortification enough to those proud men), but really to discover the greatest malice and wilfulness. What Christ did by his wisdom, we must labour to do by our well doing—<hi type="italic">put to silence the ignorance of foolish men,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.15">1 Pet. ii. 15</reference>. (2.) Christ came off with honour, and justified himself in refusing to give them an answer to their imperious demand; <hi type="italic">Neither tell I you by what authority I do these things.</hi> They did not deserve to be told; for it was plain that they contended not for truth, but victory; nor did <hi type="italic">he</hi> need to <hi type="italic">tell them,</hi> for the works which he did, told them plainly that he had authority from God to do what he did; since no man could do those miracles which he did unless God were with him. Let them wait but three or four days, and his resurrection shall tell them who gave him his authority, for by that he will be <hi type="italic">declared to be the Son of God with power,</hi> as by their rejecting of him, notwithstanding, they will be declared to be the enemies of God.  <chapter eID="Mark.11"/> <div eID="gen24813" type="x-p"/>

entries.a43332060c584929fc98192c18fa04f82ad76efe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14089"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 11</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mark.11.1-Mark.11.11">Mr 11:1-11</reference>. Christ's Triumphal Entry into Jerusalem, on the First Day of the Week. ( = <reference osisRef="Matt.21.1-Matt.21.9">Mt 21:1-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.19.29-Luke.19.40">Lu 19:29-40</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.12">Joh 12:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.12.19">19</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen27195" type="x-p"/> See on <reference osisRef="Luke.19.29-Luke.19.40">Lu 19:29-40</reference>.<div eID="gen27195" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mark.11.11-Mark.11.26">Mr 11:11-26</reference>. The Barren Fig Tree Cursed with Lessons from It--Second Cleansing of the Temple, on the Second and Third Days of the Week. ( =</title> <div sID="gen27196" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Matt.21.12-Matt.21.22">Mt 21:12-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.19.45-Luke.19.48">Lu 19:45-48</reference>).<div eID="gen27196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27197" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14089"/><hi type="bold">11. And Jesus entered into Jerusalem, and into the temple: and when he had looked round about upon--</hi>surveyed.<div eID="gen27197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27198" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all things, and now the eventide was come, he went out into Bethany with the twelve--</hi>Thus briefly does our Evangelist dispose of this His first day in Jerusalem, after the triumphal entry. Nor do the Third and Fourth Gospels give us more light. But from Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.10">Mt 21:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.14-Matt.11.16">11, 14-16</reference>) we learn some additional and precious particulars, for which see on <reference osisRef="Luke.19.45-Luke.19.48">Lu 19:45-48</reference>. It was not now safe for the Lord to sleep in the city, nor, from the day of His Triumphal Entry, did He pass one night in it, save the last fatal one.<div eID="gen27198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27199" type="x-p"/> The Barren Fig Tree Cursed (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.12-Mark.11.14">Mr 11:12-14</reference>). <div eID="gen27199" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ee6464bcb31f69ff6851015b07cfe58fc14b073: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14090"/><div sID="gen27200" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14090"/><hi type="bold">12. And on the morrow--</hi>The Triumphal Entry being on the first day of the week, this following day was Monday.<div eID="gen27200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27201" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when they were come from Bethany--</hi>"in the morning" (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.18">Mt 21:18</reference>).<div eID="gen27201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27202" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he was hungry--</hi>How was that? Had he stolen forth from that dear roof at Bethany to the "mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God?" (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.12">Lu 6:12</reference>); or, "in the morning," as on a former occasion, "risen up a great while before day, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed" (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.35">Mr 1:35</reference>); not breaking His fast thereafter, but bending His steps straight for the city, that He might "work the works of Him that sent Him while it was day?" (<reference osisRef="John.9.4">Joh 9:4</reference>). We know not, though one lingers upon and loves to trace out the every movement of that life of wonders. One thing, however we are sure of--it was real bodily hunger which He now sought to allay by the fruit of this fig tree, "if haply He might find any thing thereon"; not a mere scene for the purpose of teaching a lesson, as some early heretics maintained, and some still seem virtually to hold. <div eID="gen27202" type="x-p"/>
entries.fbe4ef9ec1df3b9fec590ee3e19d106a66a4d7d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14091"/><div sID="gen27203" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14091"/><hi type="bold">13. And seeing a fig tree--</hi>(In <reference osisRef="Matt.21.19">Mt 21:19</reference>, it is "one fig tree," but the sense is the same as here, "a certain fig tree," as in <reference osisRef="Matt.8.19">Mt 8:19</reference>, &c.). Bethphage, which adjoined Bethany, derives its name from its being a fig region--"House of figs."<div eID="gen27203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27204" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">afar off having leaves--</hi>and therefore promising fruit, which in the case of figs come before the leaves.<div eID="gen27204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27205" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he came, if haply he might find any thing thereon: and when he came to it, he found nothing but leaves; for the time of figs was not yet--</hi>What the precise import of this explanation is, interpreters are not agreed. Perhaps all that is meant is, that as the proper fig season had not arrived, no fruit would have been expected even of this tree but for the leaves which it had, which were in this case prematurely and unnaturally developed. <div eID="gen27205" type="x-p"/>
entries.1f7c7f239df170b69eb5e92a9e528e779a9cd9cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14092"/><div sID="gen27206" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14092"/><hi type="bold">14. And Jesus answered and said unto it, No man eat fruit of thee hereafter for ever--</hi>That word did not make the tree barren, but sealed it up in its own barrenness. See on <reference osisRef="Matt.13.13-Matt.13.15">Mt 13:13-15</reference>.<div eID="gen27206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27207" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And his disciples heard it--</hi>and marked the saying. This is introduced as a connecting link, to explain what was afterwards to be said on the subject, as the narrative has to proceed to the other transactions of this day.<div eID="gen27207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27208" type="x-p"/> Second Cleansing of the Temple (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.15-Mark.11.18">Mr 11:15-18</reference>).<div eID="gen27208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27209" type="x-p"/> For the exposition of this portion, see on <reference osisRef="Luke.19.45-Luke.19.48">Lu 19:45-48</reference>.<div eID="gen27209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27210" type="x-p"/> Lessons from the Cursing of the Fig Tree (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.20-Mark.11.26">Mr 11:20-26</reference>). <div eID="gen27210" type="x-p"/>
entries.4cf54e562da8048a0e67d56c26eb99b709c84247: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14093"/><div sID="gen27211" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14093"/><hi type="bold">20. And in the morning--</hi>of Tuesday, the third day of the week: He had slept, as during all this week, at Bethany.<div eID="gen27211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27212" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as they passed by--</hi>going into Jerusalem again.<div eID="gen27212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27213" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they saw the fig tree dried up from the roots--</hi>no partial blight, leaving life in the root; but it was now dead, root and branch. In <reference osisRef="Matt.21.19">Mt 21:19</reference> it is said it withered away as soon as it was cursed. But the full blight had not appeared probably at once; and in the dusk perhaps, as they returned to Bethany, they had not observed it. The precision with which Mark distinguishes the days is not observed by Matthew, intent only on holding up the truths which the incident was designed to teach. In Matthew the whole is represented as taking place at once, just as the two stages of Jairus' daughter--dying and dead--are represented by him as one. The only difference is between a more summary and a more detailed narrative, each of which only confirms the other. <div eID="gen27213" type="x-p"/>
entries.435a0a4bf1c6e2b5a1894df6beb8f7f66fc3f48b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14094"/><div sID="gen27214" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14094"/><hi type="bold">21. And Peter calling to remembrance saith unto him--</hi>satisfied that a miracle so very peculiar--a miracle, not of blessing, as all His other miracles, but of cursing--could not have been wrought but with some higher reference, and fully expecting to hear something weighty on the subject.<div eID="gen27214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27215" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Master, behold, the fig tree which thou cursedst is withered away--</hi>so connecting the two things as to show that he traced the death of the tree entirely to the curse of his Lord. Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.20">Mt 21:20</reference>) gives this simply as a general exclamation of surprise by the disciples "how soon" the blight had taken effect. <div eID="gen27215" type="x-p"/>
entries.133c9348f614a955e77722b76e0cb9bfb89db66d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14095"/><div sID="gen27216" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14095"/>22. And Jesus answering saith unto them, Have faith in God. <div eID="gen27216" type="x-p"/>
entries.0eda723e6311e406bfeaec031e68092dc1e36f8b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14096"/><div sID="gen27217" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14096"/><hi type="bold">23. For verily I say unto you, That whosoever shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed ... he shall have whatsoever he saith--</hi>Here is the lesson now. From the nature of the case supposed--that they might wish a mountain removed and cast into the sea, a thing far removed from anything which they could be thought actually to desire--it is plain that not physical but moral obstacles to the progress of His kingdom were in the Redeemer's view, and that what He designed to teach was the great lesson, that no obstacle should be able to stand before a confiding faith in God. <div eID="gen27217" type="x-p"/>
entries.553a428df492d8745910a985cb4191bba7b51e32: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14097"/><div sID="gen27218" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14097"/><hi type="bold">24. Therefore I say unto you, What things soever ye desire, when ye pray, believe that ye receive them, and ye shall have them--</hi>This verse only generalizes the assurance of <reference osisRef="Mark.11.23">Mr 11:23</reference>; which seems to show that it was designed for the special encouragement of evangelistic and missionary efforts, while this is a directory for prevailing prayer in general. <div eID="gen27218" type="x-p"/>
entries.600edf38a44f16f480012dea6c6c85bfa5d348a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14098"/><div sID="gen27219" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14098"/><hi type="bold">25. And when ye stand praying, forgive, if ye have aught against any; that your Father also which is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses, &c.--</hi>This is repeated from the Sermon on the Mount (see on <reference osisRef="Matt.6.12">Mt 6:12</reference>); to remind them that if this was necessary to the acceptableness of all prayer, much more when great things were to be asked and confidently expected. <div eID="gen27219" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14099"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mark.11.27-Mark.11.33">Mr 11:27-33</reference>. entries.56312e135067189a43a67227fcbd44d526cc06ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen39528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39529" type="x-p"/> Whereon never man sat - No animal was allowed to be employed in sacred uses, even among the heathen, that had previously been used for any domestic or agricultural purpose; and those which had never been yoked were considered as sacred. See several proofs of this in the note on <reference osisRef="Num.19.2">Num 19:2</reference> (note), and add this from Ovid: - <div eID="gen39529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39530" type="x-p"/> Bos tibi, Phoebus ait, solis occurret in arvis, <div eID="gen39530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39531" type="x-p"/> Nullum passa jugum curvique immunis aratri <div eID="gen39531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39532" type="x-p"/> Met. lib. iii. v. 10 <div eID="gen39532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39533" type="x-p"/> The Delphic oracles this answer give: - <div eID="gen39533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39534" type="x-p"/> Behold among the fields a lonely cow, <div eID="gen39534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39535" type="x-p"/> Unworn with yokes, unbroken to the plough.
entries.aaf5111e94df7453ae2e652b13a755ae295af823: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen39535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39536" type="x-p"/> And straightway he will send him hither - From the text, I think it is exceedingly plain, that our Lord did not beg, but borrow, the colt; therefore the latter clause of this verse should be understood as the promise of returning him. Some eminent critics take the same view of the passage.

Griesbach leaves it out. <div eID="gen39538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39539" type="x-p"/> Hosanna in the highest! - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.21.9">Mat 21:9</reference> (note).
entries.1a379447e5b28bd2c1a81ca24552774d2de3753e: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen39539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39540" type="x-p"/> When he had looked round about upon all things - He examined every thing - to see if the matters pertaining to the Divine worship were properly conducted; to see that nothing was wanting - nothing superfluous. <div eID="gen39540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39541" type="x-p"/> And now the eventide was come - The time in which he usually left Jerusalem, to go to Bethany.
entries.f1e944eea5d651a6def96d956e1713f8a0be02f1: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen39541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39542" type="x-p"/> For the time of figs was not yet - Rather, For it was not the season of gathering figs yet. This I am fully persuaded is the true sense of this passage, ου γαρ ην καιρος συκων. For a proof that καιρος here signifies the time of gathering the figs, see the Lxx. in <reference osisRef="Psa.1.3">Psa 1:3</reference>. He bringeth forth his fruit, εν καιρω αυτου, in his season; i.e. in the time in which fruit should be ripe, and fit for gathering. See also <reference osisRef="Mar.12.2">Mar 12:2</reference> : - And at the season, τῳ καιρῳ, the time of gathering the fruits of the vineyard. <reference osisRef="Mat.21.34">Mat 21:34</reference> : - When the time of the fruit drew near; ὁ καιρος των καρπων, the time in which the fruits were to be gathered, for it was then that the Lord of the vineyard sent his servants to receive the fruits; i.e. so much of them as the holder of the vineyard was to pay to the owner by way of rent; for in those times rent was paid in kind. <div eID="gen39542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39543" type="x-p"/> To the above may be added, <reference osisRef="Job.5.26">Job 5:26</reference> : - Thou shalt come to thy grave in Full Age, like as a shock of corn cometh in his season; κατα καιρον, in the time in which it should be reaped. <div eID="gen39543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39544" type="x-p"/> When our Lord saw this fig tree by the way-side, apparently flourishing, he went to it to gather some of the figs: being on the way-side, it was not private, but public property; and any traveler had an equal right to its fruit. As it was not as yet the time for gathering in the fruits, and yet about the time when they were ready to be gathered, our Lord with propriety expected to find some. But as this happened about five days before that passover on which Christ suffered, and the passover that year fell on the beginning of April, it has been asked, "How could our Lord expect to find ripe figs in the end of March?" Answer, Because figs were ripe in Judea as early as the passover. Besides, the fig tree puts forth its fruit first, and afterwards its leaves. Indeed, this tree, in the climate which is proper for it, has fruit on it all the year round, as I have often seen. All the difficulty in the text may be easily removed by considering that the climate of Judea is widely different from that of Great Britain. The summer begins there in March, and the harvest at the passover, as all travelers into those countries testify; therefore, as our Lord met with this tree five days before the passover, it is evident, - 1st. That it was the time of ripe figs: and, 2ndly. That it was not the time of gathering them, because this did not begin till the passover, and the transaction here mentioned took place five days before. <div eID="gen39544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39545" type="x-p"/> For farther satisfaction on this point, let us suppose: - <div eID="gen39545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39546" type="x-p"/> I. That this tree was intended to point out the state of the Jewish people. <div eID="gen39546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39547" type="x-p"/> 1. They made a profession of the true religion. <div eID="gen39547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39548" type="x-p"/> 2. They considered themselves the peculiar people of God, and despised and reprobated all others. <div eID="gen39548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39549" type="x-p"/> 3. They were only hypocrites, having nothing of religion but the profession - leaves, and no fruit. <div eID="gen39549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39550" type="x-p"/> II. That our Lord's conduct towards this tree is to be considered as emblematical of the treatment and final perdition which was to come upon this hypocritical and ungodly nation. <div eID="gen39550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39551" type="x-p"/> 1. It was a proper time for them to have borne fruit: Jesus had been preaching the doctrine of repentance and salvation among them for more than three years; the choicest influences of Heaven had descended upon them; and every thing was done in this vineyard that ought to be done, in order to make it fruitful. <div eID="gen39551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39552" type="x-p"/> 2. The time was now at hand in which God would require fruit, good fruit; and, if it did not produce such, the tree should be hewn down by the Roman axe. <div eID="gen39552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39553" type="x-p"/> Therefore, <div eID="gen39553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39554" type="x-p"/> 1. The tree is properly the Jewish nation. <div eID="gen39554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39555" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ's curse the sentence of destruction which had now gone out against it; and, <div eID="gen39555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39556" type="x-p"/> 3. Its withering away, the final and total ruin of the Jewish state by the Romans. <div eID="gen39556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39557" type="x-p"/> His cursing the fig tree was not occasioned by any resentment at being disappointed at not finding fruit on it, but to point out unto his disciples the wrath which was coming upon a people who had now nearly filled up the measure of their iniquity. <div eID="gen39557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39558" type="x-p"/> A fruitless soul, that has had much cultivation bestowed on it, may expect to be dealt with as God did with this unrighteous nation. See on <reference osisRef="Mat.21.19">Mat 21:19</reference> (note), etc.
entries.8062f78baada952d492a3322820ca5c33fc429ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen39558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39559" type="x-p"/> And they come - Several MSS. and versions have παλιν, again. This was the next day after our Lord's triumphant entry into Jerusalem; for on the evening of that day he went to Bethany, and lodged there, <reference osisRef="Mar.11.11">Mar 11:11</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Mat.21.17">Mat 21:17</reference>, and returned the next morning to Jerusalem.
entries.14c1660a3d0c2c798b35b44ec720ab544bcf6ee2: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen39559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39560" type="x-p"/> Should carry any vessel - Among the Jews the word כלי keli, vessel, had a vast latitude of meaning; it signified arms, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.4">Jer 21:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.9.1">Eze 9:1</reference>; clothes, <reference osisRef="Deu.22.5">Deu 22:5</reference>, and instruments of music, <reference osisRef="Psa.71.22">Psa 71:22</reference>. It is likely that the evangelist uses the Greek word σκευος in the same sense, and by it points out any of the things which were bought and sold in the temple.
entries.58db7db4d19d6d35ceac4a639b942f95af16249f: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen39560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39561" type="x-p"/> And he taught - them - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.21.12">Mat 21:12</reference> (note).
entries.ac0e8ddad4e83a2caa6b48746142ff183fdfc396: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen39561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39562" type="x-p"/> He went out of the city - To go to Bethany.
entries.b0b260bf006aee6d9370d5e7500f7f0fe19382ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen39562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39563" type="x-p"/> Have faith in God - Εχετε πιϚιν θεου is a mere Hebraism: have the faith of God, i.e. have strong faith, or the strongest faith, for thus the Hebrews expressed the superlative degree; so the mountains of God mean exceeding great mountains - the hail of God, exceeding great hail, etc.
entries.8752df020e5bcf97290da55984fb55492e14b07c: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen39563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39564" type="x-p"/> When ye stand praying - This expression may mean no more than, When ye are disposed, or have a mind, to pray, i.e. whenever ye perform that duty. And it is thus used and explained in the Koran, Surat. v. ver. 7. See on <reference osisRef="Mat.21.20-Mat.21.22">Mat 21:20-22</reference> (note). But the Pharisees loved to pray standing, that they might be seen of men.
entries.d015d7184c1b15d52d05b4d2e83588647f376fd0: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen39564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39565" type="x-p"/> At the end of this verse, the 7th and 8th verses of Matthew 7. Ask and ye shall receive, etc., are added by M, and sixteen other MSS. The 26th verse is wanting in BLS, seven others, some editions, the Coptic, one Itala, and Theophylact.
entries.471927d1ce162acb8006088b3a831e94697fe6a1: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen39565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39566" type="x-p"/> See on <reference osisRef="Mat.21.23-Mat.21.27">Mat 21:23-27</reference> (note).
entries.89c204e2480f83935c3b342058c455c5bd464ea4: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen39566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39567" type="x-p"/> They feared the people - Or rather, We fear, etc. Instead of εφοβουντο, they feared; the Codex Bezae, seven others, later Syriac, Arabic, Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Vulgate, and all the Itala, read φοβουμεν, or φοβουμεθα. The common reading appearing to me quite improper. <div eID="gen39567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39568" type="x-p"/> We fear the people. Εαν, if, before ειπωμεν, we shall say, is omitted by ABCEFGHLS, and more than fifty others. Bengel leaves it out of the text, and puts a note of interrogation after Εξ ανθρωπων; and then the whole passage reads thus: But shall we say, Of men? They feared the people, etc. This change renders the adoption of φοβουμεν, we fear, unnecessary. Several critics prefer this mode of distinguishing the text. However the critics may be puzzled with the text, the scribes, chief priests, and elders were worse puzzled with our Lord's question. They must convict themselves or tell a most palpable falsehood. - They told the lie, and so escaped for the present. <div eID="gen39568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39569" type="x-p"/> 1. Envy, malice, and double dealing have always a difficult part to act, and are ultimately confounded by their own projects and ruined by their own operations. On the other hand, simplicity and sincerity are not obliged to use a mask, but always walk in a plain way. <div eID="gen39569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39570" type="x-p"/> 2. The case of the barren fig-tree which our Lord cursed has been pitifully misunderstood and misapplied. The whole account of this transaction, as stated above, I believe to be correct; it is so much in our Lord's usual manner that the propriety of it will scarcely be doubted. He was ever acting the part of the philosopher, moralist, and divine, as well as that of the Savior of sinners. In his hand, every providential occurrence and every object of nature, became a means of instruction: the stones of the desert, the lilies of the field, the fowls of heaven, the beasts of the forest, fruitful and unfruitful trees, with every ordinary occurrence, were so many grand texts, from which he preached the most illuminating and impressive sermons, for the instruction and salvation of his audience. This wisdom and condescension cannot be sufficiently admired. But shall the example of the fruitless fig tree be lost on us as well as on the Jews? God forbid! Let us therefore take heed, lest having been so long unfruitful, God should say, Let no fruit appear on thee hereafter for ever! and in consequence of this, we wither and die away! See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Mar.11.27">Mar 11:27</reference> (note).  <chapter eID="Mark.11"/> <div eID="gen39570" type="x-p"/>

entries.391efa74fbe13480bd902d686b7af651bfaf01c9:
Verse 11-26. Mt 21:18 and Mt 21:19-22

Verse 11. Into the temple. Not into the edifice properly called the temple, but into the courts which surrounded the principal edifice. Our Saviour, not being of the tribe of Levi, was not permitted to enter into the holy or most holy place; and when, therefore, it is said that he went into the temple, it is always to be understood of the courts surrounding the temple. See Mt 21:12.

And when he had looked round about upon all. Having seen or examined everything. He saw the abominations and abuses which he afterwards corrected. It may be wondered at, that he did not at once correct them, instead of waiting to another day. But it may be observed that God is slow to anger, that he does not at once smite the guilty, but waits patiently before he rebukes and chastises.

The eventide. The evening; the time after three o'clock, P.M. It is very probable that this was before sunset. The religious services of the temple closed, without the offering of the evening sacrifice, at three o'clock, P. M., and Jesus probably soon left the city.

entries.e1c57f86aa5d7111e46bca7d262be2d84906beaa:
Verse 25. And when ye stand praying. When ye pray. It seems that the posture in prayer was sometimes standing and sometimes kneeling. God looks upon the heart rather than upon our position in worship; and if the heart be right, any posture may be proper. It cannot be doubted, however, that in private, in the family, and wherever it can be conveniently done, the kneeling posture is more proper, as expressing more humility and reverence, and more in accordance with Scripture examples, Compare Ps 95:6, 2Chr 6:13, Dan 6:10, Lk 22:41, Acts 7:60, 9:40. Yet a subject like this may be regarded as of too much consequence, and we should be careful that anxiety about a mere form should not exclude anxiety about a far more important matter--the state of the soul.

entries.fa2174de2f3e858d9441cec3a50eb66c230db02d: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.11.11" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.11.11" sID="gen101411" type="section"/> <div sID="gen101412" type="x-p"/>There is a difference between Matthew and Mark in their narrative of the <hi type="italic">withering of the fig tree</hi>; for Matthew says that it was on the day after that Christ made a public appearance as King, while Mark appears to throw it back to the following day. <note n="9"> <div sID="gen101413" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que le jour ensuyvant les disciples prindrent garde à ce qui estoit advenu à l’arbre</foreign>;”— “that, on the following day, the disciples took notice of what had happened the tree.”<div eID="gen101413" type="x-p"/> </note> But the solution is easy; for they agree in this respect, that Christ, on the day after that he made his solemn entrance into the city, cursed the tree; only Mark states what Matthew had omitted, that the occurrence was observed by the disciples on the following day., So then, though Mark has stated more distinctly the order of time, he makes no contradiction.<div eID="gen101412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101414" type="x-p"/>He appears to differ more openly both from Matthew and from Luke in the narrative of chastising the traders; <note n="10"> <div sID="gen101415" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">En l’histoire des marchans chassez hors du temple</foreign>;” — “in the narrative of the merchants driven out of the temple.”<div eID="gen101415" type="x-p"/> </note> for while both of them declare that Christ, as soon as he <hi type="italic">entered into the city and temple, drove out those who sold and bought</hi>, Mark simply says that he looked around on all things, but has thrown back the driving of them out till another day. <note n="11"> <div sID="gen101416" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et puis il remet à l’autre jour ensuyvant ceste reformation du temple</foreign>;” — “and then he throws back to the other following day that reformation of the temple.”<div eID="gen101416" type="x-p"/> </note> But I reconcile them in this way, that Mark, not having spoken about the purifying of the temple, afterwards inserts it, though not in its proper place. He relates that, on the first day, Christ came into the temple, and there looked round on all things. <note n="12"> <div sID="gen101417" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et là regarda tout autour ce qui s’y faisoit</foreign>;” — “and there looked all around at what was done in it.”<div eID="gen101417" type="x-p"/> </note> Now why did he look so earnestly, except for the purpose of correcting something that was wrong? For, having been formerly accustomed to pay frequent visits to the temple, it was not the novelty of the sight that affected him. Now as Mark ought immediately to have added, that those who sold and bought in the temple were driven out of it, he says that Christ went out of the city; but, having omitted what was worthy of being related, he inserts it afterwards.<div eID="gen101414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101418" type="x-p"/>But perhaps some will be more inclined to believe that, in this narrative also, Mark observed the order of time, which the other two Evangelists had disregarded; for though they appear to indicate an uninterrupted succession of events, yet as they do not name a particular day, there would be no impropriety in dividing what we find to be connected in their writings. For my own part, however, I prefer the conjecture which I stated first; for it is probable that this demonstration of his power was made by Christ in presence of a large multitude. But any one who will consider how little care the Evangelists bestowed on pointing out dates will not stumble at this diversity in the narrative.<div eID="gen101418" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.11.11" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen101411" osisID="Mark.11.11" type="section"/>
