                     </ns0:gap>oh. 12.14.</ns0:note> Nd when they came nigh to Jerusalem, unto Bethphage, and Bethany, at the mount of Olives, he sendeth forth two of his disciples.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> saith nothing of <ns0:hi>Bethany,</ns0:hi> mentioned by <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke.</ns0:hi> It was the Town of <ns0:hi>Lazarus, Iohn</ns0:hi> 11.1. Some think that <ns0:hi>Bethany</ns0:hi> was rather a Tract of the <ns0:hi>Mount of Olives,</ns0:hi> then a Town, and that <ns0:hi>Bethphage</ns0:hi> was a kind of Suburbs to <ns0:hi>Ie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rusalem,</ns0:hi> at the remotest part of which <ns0:hi>Bethany</ns0:hi> began, but the Town it self call'd <ns0:hi>Bethany,</ns0:hi> was fifteen Furlongs, near two Miles from <ns0:hi>Ierusalem.</ns0:hi> It was the place from which Christ A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />scended to Heaven, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 24.50. A Sabbath Days Journey from <ns0:hi>Ierusalem, Acts</ns0:hi> 1.12. at some distance from the Town called <ns0:hi>Bethany,</ns0:hi> from this place called still <ns0:hi>Bethany,</ns0:hi> upon the Borders of <ns0:hi>Bethphage,</ns0:hi> he sent out two of his disciples.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 And saith unto them, <ns0:note place="margin">Mat. 21.2. Luke 19.30.</ns0:note> Go your way into the village over against you; and assoon as ye be entred into it, ye shall find a colt tied, whereon never man sate, loose him, and bring <ns0:hi>him.</ns0:hi>
                  <ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> saith <ns0:hi>an Ass with a Colt.</ns0:hi> The other Evangelists speak only of the <ns0:hi>Colt.</ns0:hi> The Heathens by a Light of Na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture, shewing them there was a Reverence and Honour due to the Divine Being, were wont in the use they made of Creatures for any Divine Service, to use such as they had not before used, for common uses; the Philistines, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 6.7. sending home the Ark, set it on a <ns0:hi>new C<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>t,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>took two Milch Kine, on which there never came Yoke.</ns0:hi> But our Saviour probably made choice of such a Colt, for the further notice of the Miracle (Colts being when first Backed more unruly) or for some other wise end which we know not.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 And if any man say unto you, Why do ye this? say ye that the Lord hath need of him, and straight<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />way he will send him hither.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 And they went their way, and found the colt tied by the door without, in a place where two ways met, and they loose him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 And certain of them that stood there, said un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to them, what do ye loosing the colt?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 And they said unto them even as Jesus had com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />manded, and they let him go.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 20.18.19. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> All along the Story of our Saviours Life and Actions, we shall find certain In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dications of his Divine Power and Vertue. His <ns0:hi>knowing Mens thoughts,</ns0:hi> and declarations of such his Knowledge to them. His certain Prediction of future Contingencies, being able to tell Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sons such particulars as no Man could know; how could he who was not God, have told the Disciples, that at their entrance into the Village, they should find a Colt, on which never Man sate, that the owners would not resist Strangers to take it away? Yet not<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />withstanding all this his Disciples very imperfectly believed him to be so, until he was risen from the Dead. The time was not yet come when Christ would have this Published, and while he gave them a Power to believe it, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> to have a full persuasion of it, all these Moral Arguments, were not sufficient to work in their Hearts a full persuasion. The Faith of the Christians of that time, seemeth to have had these three Gradations. 1. They <ns0:hi>believed him a great Prophet,</ns0:hi> that had received great Power from God. 2. They owned him <ns0:hi>as the</ns0:hi> Messiah, <ns0:hi>as the Son of</ns0:hi> David, and now and then they would drop some Expressions, ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />guing some persuasions that he was the <ns0:hi>Son of God.</ns0:hi> 3. Last of all, <ns0:hi>they came to a firm persuasion that he was truly God,</ns0:hi> as well as Man; after that he was risen from the Dead, and decla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red with Power to be such as the Apostle saith, yet what means imaginable could they have had more then, 1. A Voice from Heaven declaring it. 2. The Spirits descending in a Visible Shape. 3. The great Miracles he had wrought by Sea and Land, commanding the Winds and the Waves, healing incurable Di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />seases, and all others in an instant, without use of Rational Means, raising the Dead, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> 4. His telling their thoughts, fore<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />telling future Contingencies, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> yet all these produced in the Generality of the People no more than Amazement, and Asto<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nishments in the Apostles themselves, rather a Disposition to such a Faith, or an Opinion or Suspicion of such a thing, than a firm and fixed persuasion concerning it.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 19.35.36.</ns0:note> And they brought the colt to Jesus, and cast their garments on him; and he sate upon him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 And many spread their garments in the way, and others cut down branches off the trees, and strow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> in the way.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 And they that went before, and they that fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowed, cryed, saying, Hosanna, Blessed <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> he that co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />meth in the name of the Lord.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 Blessed <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> the kingdom of our father David, that cometh in the name of the Lord, Hosanna in the highest.<ns0:note place="bottom">We met with all this <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 21. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 8, 9. see the Notes there. It appeareth by our Saviour sending for the <ns0:hi>Colt,</ns0:hi> that this little Rural Triumph, and the Acclamations attending it were designed by him, hoth to shew the People, 1. <ns0:hi>That he was the King whom God had promised to set upon his holy Hill of</ns0:hi> Zion, and 2. <ns0:hi>That his Kingdom was not of this World.</ns0:hi> For (as he elsewhere saith) if his <ns0:hi>Kingdom had been of this World, his Ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vants would have Fought for him.</ns0:hi> So it may be said, you may know his Kingdom that he spake of, <ns0:hi>was not of this World</ns0:hi>; for if i<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> had there would have been found a more stately Beast than the <ns0:hi>Colt of an Ass,</ns0:hi> or at least a Saddle for that; the ways would have been covered with Tapestry, rather then poor Mens <ns0:hi>Coats</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Cloaks,</ns0:hi> and other <ns0:hi>Heralds</ns0:hi> would have been found, than a Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pany of <ns0:hi>Children,</ns0:hi> and poor Men crying <ns0:hi>Hosanna.</ns0:hi> This was such a thing as would but have Ridiculed a <ns0:hi>Government</ns0:hi> to be a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fraid of, nor indeed (to give <ns0:hi>Pontius Pilate</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Roman Governour</ns0:hi> at this time in <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> his due) do we find him the least disturb'd, tho the <ns0:hi>Scribes</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> (which were the Jewish Church-men) seeing their Kingdom going down were something netled, and tho they had more Modesty than to bring this little <ns0:hi>Triumph</ns0:hi> in judgment against him, yet their great charge was, his declaring and making himself a <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> In order to which this was the great<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est shew he ever made.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 19.45</ns0:note> And Jesus entred into Jerusalem, and into the temple; and when he had looked round about up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on all things, and now the even-tide was come, he went out unto Bethany with the twelve.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 21.18.</ns0:note> And on the morrow, when they were come from Bethany, he was hungry.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 And seeing a fig-tree afar off, having leaves, he came, if haply he might find any thing thereon, and when he came to it he found nothing but leaves, for the time of figs was not <ns0:hi>yet.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 And Jesue answered and said unto it, No man eat fruit of thee hereafter for ever. And his disciples heard <ns0:hi>it.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:287" />15 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 19.45.</ns0:note> And they come to Jerusalem, And Jesus went into the temple, and began to cast out them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the money-changers, and the seats of them that sold doves.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 And would not suffer that any man should car<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry any vessel though the temple.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 And he taught, saying unto them, Is it not written, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 56.7.</ns0:note> My house shall be called <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>an house of prayer, for all nations.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> of all nations, the house of prayer? but <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jer. 7.11.</ns0:note> ye have made it a den of thieves.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 And the scribes and chief priests heard <ns0:hi>it,</ns0:hi> and sought <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 19.47.</ns0:note> how they might destroy him, for they fear<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed him, because all the people was astonished at his doctrine.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 And when even was come, he went out of the city.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the <ns0:hi>Notes</ns0:hi> on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 21.12. where having so largely spoken to this part of the History, considering also what <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> hath to compleat the History, few Words will be need<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful about it here. Tho <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> seems to relate it so, as if the first Day Christ came into the <ns0:hi>Temple,</ns0:hi> lookt about it, and did no more till he came back from <ns0:hi>Bethany</ns0:hi> (whither he went that Night) <ns0:hi>the next Day,</ns0:hi> yet the other Evangelists Relation of it, would make one think otherwise, besides that Interpreters think it not probable, that our Saviour the first Night, should only look about, and patiently see and suffer those abuses; most do therefore think, that our Saviour the first Day did cast out those that <ns0:hi>sold and bought in the Temple.</ns0:hi> In the Notes upon <ns0:hi>Mat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thew</ns0:hi> we have given an account of the Market in the <ns0:hi>Court of the Gentiles,</ns0:hi> which was the outward Court of the Temple, where through the Covetousness of the Priests, some say there were con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stant Shops. In the Temple there were, The most <ns0:hi>Holy place</ns0:hi> (into which the Priests only entred) and the <ns0:hi>Holy place</ns0:hi> into which entred all the <ns0:hi>Circumcised,</ns0:hi> whether Native <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Proselytes.</ns0:hi> These two places they accounted <ns0:hi>Holy.</ns0:hi> But there was also a <ns0:hi>Court</ns0:hi> which they called the <ns0:hi>Court of the Gentiles,</ns0:hi> of which they had no such esteem, but allowed the keeping of Shops and Markets in it, e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />specially before the Passover. Concerning our Saviour's driving out these Buyers and Sellers, see the <ns0:hi>Notes</ns0:hi> on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 21.12, 13. In those Notes also I have fully opened the History concerning our Saviours Cursing the Barren Fig-Tree, and given what ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />count Interpreters do give of the difficulty arising from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 13. as to which I have nothing to add here, save this only, of<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fering it to Learned Persons to consider, Whether the Sense of these Words <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, be any more than<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>for there were no Figs. He found nothing but Leaves, for there were no Figs,</ns0:hi> as if it had been <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. So as <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> there should neither signify, the common time when Figs use to be ripe, nor yet signify, the seasonableness of the Year for Figs, but particularly relate to that Tree, which at that time had no Figs. But enough hath been before said, as to that Text.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 21.20.21.</ns0:note>20 And in the morning as they passed by, they saw the fig-tree dryed up from the roots.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 And Peter calling to remembrance, saith un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to him, Master, behold, the fig-tree which thou cursedst, is withered away.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 And Jesus answering, saith unto them, Have faith <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>of God.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> in God.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 For verily I say unto you, that whosoever shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea, and shall not doubt in his heart, but shall believe that those things which he saith, shall come to pass, he shall have whatsoever he saith.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the <ns0:hi>Notes</ns0:hi> on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 20.21. It is I confess the opinion of many excellent Interpreters, whom I Reverence, that the main end of our Saviours Cursing, and Blasting this Fig-tree, was to let his Disciples see in a Type, what would be the Consequent of a Spiritual Barrenness. That Spiritual Barrenness is exceeding dan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gerous, is out of question; our Saviour teacheth it us plainly by another Parable of the Fig-tree, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 13.7, 8.9. and the A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />postle teacheth us it, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 6.7, 8. But I see nothing to Guide us to any such Interpretation of this Action of his, which was a Mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />raculous operation by which, as he, 1. plainly shewed his Divine Po<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wer. So 2. these Verses inform us, that it was his design to shew his People the Power of <ns0:hi>Faith,</ns0:hi> that is, a <ns0:hi>full persuasion, that what<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />soever we ask of God according to his Will, and which may tend to his Glory, shall be done for us.</ns0:hi> Which Interpretation of this Action of our Saviours, solves all the difficulties relating to this Story, about which Interpreters have so disquieted them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 Therefore I say unto you, <ns0:note place="margin">Mat. 7.7. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 21.22. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 11.5.</ns0:note> What things soe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver ye desire when ye pray, believe that ye receive <ns0:hi>them,</ns0:hi> and ye shall have <ns0:hi>them.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 And when ye stand praying, <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 16.24. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 1.6, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 6.14.</ns0:note> forgive, if ye have ought against any, that your Father also which is in heaven may forgive you your tres<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />passes.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father which is in heaven forgive your trespasses.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 21.22. and <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 7.7. and <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 6.14. In which Texts we before met with what we have in these Verses, teaching us the necess<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ty of <ns0:hi>Faith,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Charity</ns0:hi> to those who would so pray as to find acceptance with God. This also lets us know the necessity of Peoples full Satisfaction, that what things they ask of God in Prayer, are according to the Will of God, without which it is not possible they should pray, with a full persuasion that they shall receive, whatsoever they in Prayer ask of God. And because it is impossible we should in this point be fully satisfyed, without a Divine Revelation, as to things not necessary to Salvation, our Faith or Persuasion can rise no higher, than a <ns0:hi>full persuasion, that if things of this nature, when we ask them of God in Prayer, be such as are for our good, and for Gods Glory, we shall receive them.</ns0:hi> The cause was otherwise as to those to whom Christ had given a Power to work Miracles; what they asked of that Nature, they must know it was the Will of God to effect by them, and they could not without Sin doubt of it.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 And they come again to Jerusalem, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 21.22.</ns0:note> and as he was walking in the temple, there come to him the chief priests, and the scribes, and the elders.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 And say unto him, By what authority dost thou these things? and who gave thee this authori<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty to do these things?<ns0:note place="bottom">Our Lord went every Night to <ns0:hi>Bethany</ns0:hi> (two Miles or near so much) and returned in the Morning to <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi>; our Savi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />our walkt, and taught in the Temple. <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> saith the <ns0:hi>Priests</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Scribes</ns0:hi> came to him as he was teaching. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith, as he was walking, possibly he at the same time both <ns0:hi>walked</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>taught,</ns0:hi> for in his whole Story we shall observe that he lost no time, if he were walking by the High-way, or sitting in the House, where ever he was, we still find him teaching; see the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 21. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 23. where we had the same thing.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 And Jesus answered and said unto them, I will also ask of you one <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>thing.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> question, and answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 The baptisme of John, was it from heaven, or <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 20.3, 4, 5, 6.</ns0:note> of men? answer me.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 And they reasoned with themselves, saying, If we shall say, From heaven, he will say, Why then did ye not believe him?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 But if we shall say, Of men, they feared the people, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat 14.5. Chap. 6.20.</ns0:note> for all men counted John, that he was a prophet indeed.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 And they answered and said unto Jesus, We cannot tell. And Jesus answering, saith unto them, Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 21. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 24, 25, 26, 27, where are the same passages opened. A Prophet here, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 32. signifyeth, one extraordinarily inspired, and sent of God to reveal his Will, so as his <ns0:hi>Baptisme</ns0:hi> must needs be from Heaven. This Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />putation<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> it seems Universally had, so as to have denied his Baptisme to have been from Heaven, had been to have exposed themselves to the Mockings, if not the rage of the People, which they were loth to do. If they had said from <ns0:hi>Heaven,</ns0:hi> they had accu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed themselves for not believing him, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 7.48. This makes them chuse rather to make themselves doubtful in the Case. And giveth our Saviour a fitting occasion to deny them Satis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />faction, as to what they asked of him.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
